title: Who Will Wire the Future? Why America Needs a New Generation of Electricians
body_markdown:
NEWS ARTICLE


Who Will Wire the Future? Why America Needs a New Generation of Electricians


*By Brian Coleman, President of Electrical Connections, nVent*


Imagine it: you’re an electrical subcontractor working on large grid substation or data center build; deadlines are tight and you’re scrambling to find enough qualified electricians. Your crews are working 10–12 hour days for months. Pressure is building. So is exhaustion.


Many subcontractors don’t have to use their imagination. This is the reality they live with every day, as society builds the nation’s AI infrastructure while simultaneously tackling electrical grid upgrades and other large-scale electrification projects. Subcontractors are asking a simple question with growing urgency: who’s going to do the work?


There is a structural shortage of electricians in the U.S, and it’s getting worse. According to one[estimate](https://qmerit.com/blog/electrician-shortage-what-it-means-for-electrical-contractors/) , almost 10,000 electricians exit the field each year while only about 7,000 new workers enter it. This shortage is hampering the data center boom and the modernization of the power grid. It’s also leaving unfilled good jobs that can provide a prosperous future for a new generation of workers.


**Defining the Problem**


Long-established trends are responsible for the shortfall. A cultural bias toward four-year college degrees is starving the trades of new entrants. Not enough students are exposed to high‑skill, high‑wage trades like electrical work as real career options. As a result, community college and trade‑school pipelines aren’t supplying nearly enough new workers. And new entrants often arrive on the job with less experience, even as projects grow larger and more complex.


Next, consider the other side of the equation: soaring demand for electrical work. AI, cloud computing, and digital services are driving a massive data‑center build‑out. Each type of facility requires electrical systems and power architecture. At the same time, the U.S. grid is aging and needs to be expanded and modernized to handle more load and integrate renewable energy sources. Indeed, by some[estimates](https://www.nlr.gov/news/feature/2024/national-transmission-planning-study) , the grid could double in size or more by 2050.


This adds up to intense competition for — and strain on — a limited pool of licensed electricians, who must often work long shifts far from home, leading to burnout and making retention harder.


It also means that those starting work now will likely enjoy a long-term career with steady work. The responsibility for maintaining and upgrading the grid will continue for decades.


The bad news: if we fail to replenish the ranks of skilled electricians, we risk a future of delayed or over‑budget infrastructure projects, slower deployment of clean energy, and potential reliability and safety challenges in critical facilities.


**Powering Tomorrow**


The first step in training and growing the workforce is revitalizing trade and technical education. I recommend three related approaches:


- Renewing investment in career and technical education (CTE), community colleges, and specialized electrical programs. This shouldn’t happen in a vacuum, but rather through closer collaboration between industry and educators so students train on real‑world equipment and standards.


- Recommitting to apprenticeships and on‑the‑job learning, especially apprenticeship programs that pay people while they learn. At my company, nVent, we offer apprenticeship programs for employees to gain skilled trades inside our facilities. We also partner with local electrical trade schools, where students train using nVent products and systems. It’s an excellent way to broaden the talent pool, attracting more young people, more women, and more underrepresented groups.


- Elevating the perception of the trade. Being an electrician isn’t just a great career; it’s a noble profession. Our society simply couldn’t run without them. We must do everything within our power to recast electrical work as essential to the digital and clean‑energy economy. It’s well‑paid and stable over a 20- or 30-year horizon.


Fortunately, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) aligns with and champions all three of these goals through its workforce development initiatives. It also supports the Veterans Energy Transition (VET) Act, which proposes[transferring up to $500,000 to employers to subsidize the hiring and retraining of retired military personnel into skilled trade roles](https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/nema-other-groups-want-the-us-to-pay-companies-to-employ-veterans-as-elect/813045/) . I encourage all electrical contractors to support these goals and leverage NEMA’s workforce development resources.


**Smarter, Simpler, Safer Products**


nVent is tackling this problem from another angle as well. Becoming a qualified journeyman electrician typically takes years. Most electricians complete a four- to five-year apprenticeship that combines classroom instruction with thousands of hours of hands-on field experience before earning journeyman credentials. That’s not an accident — the work is rigorous and requires extreme operational discipline.


One way that nVent is making the job a bit less complex is by designing products that are more intuitive and standardized as well as safer, faster, and easier to install. This philosophy reduces the burden on scarce, ultra‑specialized labor and requires less time spent troubleshooting in the field.


We’re also building more finished systems and customized solutions that arrive on the job site ready to go, empowering less experienced workers to do high‑quality work under the guidance of more senior electricians. As an added benefit, this approach minimizes the need for specialized field fabrication.


Finally, nVent works with customers to gather input for new solutions, creating an innovation feedback loop.


**All Hands on Deck**


It’s time for a concerted, nationwide effort. Policymakers and educators must treat the electrician shortage as a strategic national issue, on par with other infrastructure priorities. They must invest in the training ecosystem, from high school CTE programs to apprenticeships and upskilling.


Manufacturers and contractors can help themselves by building or extending apprenticeship and training pathways inside their own facilities. They can partner with trade schools and community colleges to create a steady talent pipeline.


If we want a resilient, modern, and sustainable grid, we first have to invest in the people who build it.
